newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish inflation set to meet EMU needs - economists.
newsitem.headline: Irish inflation set to meet EMU needs - economists.

text.p: Ireland looks set to comfortably meet Maastricht inflation requirements after the February consumer price index, published on Thursday, showed a surprisingly low figure for the second month in a row, economists said.
Maastricht requires inflation for qualifying countries to be within 1.5 percent of the average of the lowest three rates.
Economists said Ireland looks set to sail home on that front with annual inflation now expected to come in under the 2.0 percent in 1997.
The February consumer price index (CPI), published by the Central Statistics Office (CSO), showed a rise of 0.6 percent month-on-month, giving a year-on-year increase of 1.5 percent.
This compared to forecasts of up to 1.0 percent rise month-on-month and 2.0 percent year-on-year.

"We will be revising our forecasts down after these numbers," Davy stockbrokers economist Michael Crowley told Reuters. "We said at the time of the January figures, which were very low, that even allowing for the special factors in January we would revise down our figures."
Davy had forecast a rise of 2.0 percent year-on-year for the February and forecast a full-year average rate of around 2.4 to 2.5 percent.

Bloxham's stockbrokers economist Alan MacQuaid, who predicted a monthly rise of 0.5 percent and a year-on-year rate of 1.5 percent, said the difficulty for analysts was that they had nothing to compare the figures with because in the past CPI data was published on a quarterly basis only.

The February data was just the second time that monthly figures have been published and followed a surprisingly low January number of a 0.5 percent monthly rise which economists, lacking comparisons, put down to distortions due to price cutting in the January sales.
"The February numbers are very good. The figures are better than we expected and we were at the low end of the range, " NCB economist Dermot O'Brien said.
O'Brien, who had forecast a year-on-year rise of 1.8 percent in February, said the important thing now was that all the scare stories about Irish inflation were not borne out.
The CSO data comes in the wake of Ireland's Central Bank's spring bulletin last week which warned against the evils of inflation, particularly in a key year for Maastricht qualification.
The Central Bank said a deceleration in consumer demand was desirable to ensure sustainable growth in the Irish economy and warned against moves which would stimulate inflationary pressures.
It estimated, in its quarterly bulletin, that an expansionary January budget, offset by an appreciating nominal exchange rate, would translate into an average inflation rate of 2.3 percent for 1997.
Economist feel, in the wake of the February data, the central bank forecast is too high.
"I think what it (the low February number) is pointing to is an inflation rate below 2.0 percent for 1997," O'Brien said.
He said on top of that the harmonised EU index was showing an improving trend for Ireland.
The European Union harmonised index of consumer prices, which is used for intra-EU comparisons, showed a rise of 1.7 percent year-on-year in February compared with 1.9 percent in January.

"... and a lot of other countries are going the other way in that the limit for the Maastricht average inflation criterion is rising," O'Brien added. "Back around November the average EU inflation number was something like 2.4 percent and in January it between 2.6 and 2.7 percent. So our headroom is increasing."
